As the field of medicine and laws have evolved since the early 1900s, the battle against misinformation has persisted. The American Medical Association
(AMA) has been at the centre of this fight. In the early 1900s, the AMA formed a Bureau of Investigation to expose and combat medical fraud, or the promotion of unsubstantiated or deceitful health claims. It published articles, pamphlets, books and posters to help consumers separate fraud from legitimate information. Its staff also toured the country to give lectures and attend state fairs, and collaborated with government agencies like the Food and Drug Administration. They answered tens of thousands of letters from doctors and ordinary Americans who were looking for more information about a particular drug that they may have seen advertised in a magazine or newspaper. Yet medical fraud continues to exist in various forms, and the spread of misinformation during the COVID-19 pandemic is among the most notable examples. With so many unknowns as the illness spread across the US, misinformation about the potential of drugs like Hydroxychloroquine to combat COVID-19 spread rapidly on the internet and social media. Helping consumers separate sense from nonsense in health and medicine starts with education, and ideally,
the strengthening of laws related to medical fraud, according to experts. Today, there are still diseases for which the medical community simply has not discovered cures, leading to despair among the public and the multi-billion-dollar pharmaceutical industry exploits that sense of fear. And as long as that gap is going to be there, there is going to be fraud.

Roman roads have long been admired for their durability and advanced construction techniques, playing an essential role in the expansion and governance of the Empire. They were more than mere routes; they were carefully designed and constructed pathways that connected cities, military outposts,
and ports across thousands of miles. Their longevity is a testament to Roman engineering prowess, with many of these roads still intact today. The Romans employed a meticulous, multi-layered process to
construct their roads, which provided both stability and durability. Roman engineers, known as agrimensores, first marked out the road route using tools which allowed for precise alignment and levelling. They aimed for direct paths, regardless of natural obstacles, which were either bridged or tunnelled through when possible. Once the path was marked, labourers would excavate a trench, which varied in depth depending on the terrain and intended use of the road. The trench was foundational, as it provided stability for the roads. Roman roads were constructed in multiple layers, each with specific materials and purposes to ensure stability and drainage. Several factors, like high-quality materials, layered structure, regular maintenance and strategic alignment contributed to the extraordinary durability of the roads. The time it took to build a road depended on several factors, like the terrain, available labour, and the urgency of the project. Generally, it could take several months to complete. However,
in challenging terrains with obstacles like rivers or
mountains, road construction would extend to several years. The Roman Empire employed a large workforce for road construction, including soldiers, local labourers, and slaves. Military engineers supervised the process to ensure a swift pace, as roads were critical for connecting new territories and securing the Empire’s borders.

Trees that have protected ancient cities for hundreds of years are being burned, slashed and bulldozed
to make way for housing and industrial agriculture. Deforestation is destroying archaeological sites really fast. That’s why archaeologists are in a race against time to discover the world’s lost ancient sites before they are destroyed. One of the latest discoveries was made by some archaeologists who were examining satellite images taken above Mexico. However, it was not initially apparent just how big the discovery was as they first thought they had discovered just one structure. But, in fact, it was a city. Named Valerina, the city is believed to have been home to thousands of people at its peak. Archaeologists predict that it contains nearly 6,500 structures. Technology is rapidly advancing the capabilities of archaeologists to locate forgotten ruins in hard-to-reach locations. As remote sensing technology improves, archaeologists have realized that it has been the forest that has protected
these ruins for so long by making them hard to access. Therefore, there is a sense of urgency about mapping these areas before the forest is destroyed and more archaeological heritage is lost forever. 56. Researchers believe the fossils they found in the cave in Northern Spain indicate that ----.
Marine fossils found in a Neanderthal cave in northern Spain suggest that extinct hominids may have shared modern humans’ habit of collecting items, just as people today collect baseball cards and souvenirs.
The practice of collecting may seem like a pretty basic behaviour, but, it is in fact, indicative of advanced cognition since it requires attributing symbolic meanings to things. The extent to which Neanderthals were capable of such abstract thought remains a topic of debate, although mounting evidence hints at their surprisingly complex imaginations. For instance, researchers point out that these ancient species produced art, cared for the elderly and disabled, and may even have developed religious practices. In most cases, these consist of just one or two items, which can be understood as evidence of an artistic interest or curiosity for the forms of nature. Dated to between
